title: Standing at a Cambodian Noodle Cart With No Small Bills? Here's Your FAQ
summary: How payments actually work at Cambodian street food stalls and markets: KHQR codes, the USD and riel confusion, small change, and how visitors can scan like locals.
body_markdown:
You find the cart. The num banh chok looks perfect, the grill smoke smells right, and the woman running it nods when you point. Then comes the part nobody prepared you for: she quotes a price in dollars, your change might come back in riel, and the printed square of paper taped to her cart is a QR code you have no idea how to use. These are the questions travelers actually type into their phones from a plastic stool in Phnom Penh, answered one at a time.


## Do street food stalls in Cambodia really take QR payments?


Yes, and far more of them than first-time visitors expect. The laminated square you see taped to carts, hung from umbrella poles, or propped against the drinks cooler is a KHQR code, Cambodia's national QR standard run through the Bakong system. It is not a niche thing for fancy cafes. The noodle lady, the sugarcane juice guy, the grilled banana stall outside the temple, most of them display one, because Cambodians themselves increasingly pay this way. If a stall takes money at all, there is a good chance it takes KHQR.


## Why does everything cost dollars but my change comes back in riel?


Cambodia runs on two currencies at once. US dollars handle most prices above a dollar or two, and Khmer riel handles everything smaller, because US coins do not circulate. So a plate of lok lak might be quoted at a round dollar figure, you hand over a bill, and your change arrives as a small stack of riel notes you now have to learn to count. There is no trick to it, it is just how the country works, and every traveler spends their first day doing slow mental math over a bowl of noodles.


The quiet upside of QR payments is that this entire dance disappears. Scan, confirm the exact amount, done. No change, no wondering whether the riel you got back adds up, no apologetic shrug because the vendor cannot break your twenty.


## Can I just pay cash and skip all of this?


You can, but cash in Cambodia comes with its own homework. Vendors inspect dollar bills and often refuse anything torn, heavily creased, or marked, which means the twenties your home bank gave you may be rejected on sight. And small change in riel is a constant low-grade hassle: you never have quite the right notes, the vendor never has quite the right change, and someone always ends up rounding. For a one-dollar iced coffee, scanning a code is simply less friction than fishing through a pocket of mixed currencies. We went deeper on the cash side of this in our guide to


[getting through a full day in Cambodia on KHQR](https://moretapay.com/blog/cambodia-khqr-payments-guide-digital-nomad-usd-riel-2026-2026-10-25)


.


## I don't have a Cambodian bank account. Can I actually scan KHQR?


This is the question that matters, because KHQR codes normally connect to local Cambodian banking apps, and you cannot open one of those as a short-term visitor. The workaround is a wallet built for exactly this gap. Moreta Pay lets you scan the same KHQR codes locals use, with money you topped up from your own bank at home, whether that is a US account via Plaid or ACH, a European SEPA transfer, UK Faster Payments, a Canadian e-Transfer, or an international card. You load the wallet in your own currency, and when you scan at the stall, the app shows the amount, the merchant name, and the FX rate before you confirm. No local account, no hidden foreign transaction markup, no guessing what the conversion actually cost you.


## What does paying at a stall actually look like, step by step?


It takes about ten seconds once you have done it twice. Order your food. The vendor either points at the printed KHQR code or holds it up. Open Moreta Pay, scan the code, check that the merchant name looks right and the amount matches what she said (for street food she usually tells you the total and you type it in, since fixed-amount codes are more of a shop thing). Confirm, then show her the success screen. Many vendors get a notification or an SMS on their own phone almost instantly, so often you do not even need to show anything. Then you sit down and eat.


## Do the big markets work the same way as street carts?


Mostly yes, with one twist. In places like Phnom Penh's Central Market, the Russian Market, or the night markets in Siem Reap, the food court sections and drink stalls are heavily QR-friendly. The souvenir and clothing stalls are too, but there you are also haggling, and the negotiated price is what you scan for. Agreeing on four dollars and then paying exactly four dollars by QR is actually cleaner than haggling and then discovering neither of you can make change. One habit to copy from locals: confirm the final number out loud before you scan, so there is no ambiguity about whether you settled in dollars or riel.


## Should I carry any cash at all?


Yes, a modest amount. Tuk tuk drivers outside the ride-hailing apps, remote village stops on a countryside tour, the occasional elderly vendor with no phone, these still want paper. Keep some small riel notes and a few clean, unworn dollar bills as backup. The realistic split for most travelers in 2026 is QR for the overwhelming majority of food, drinks, and market purchases, and a thin cash reserve for the edges. That is a much better ratio than it was even a couple of years ago, and it mirrors what we have seen across the region, from


[Thailand's PromptPay street food scene](https://moretapay.com/blog/thailand-street-food-markets-how-to-pay-promptpay-qr-cash-cards-2026-2026-10-31)


to Vietnam's laminated VietQR codes.


## What about paying for things beyond the market?


The same KHQR rails cover a lot more than noodle carts. Convenience stores, pharmacies, cafes, sit-down restaurants, and many guesthouses display the same codes, so one payment habit covers your whole day. And since Moreta Pay also handles QR-based online checkouts on platforms travelers in the region actually use, like Agoda and Trip.com, the wallet you topped up for street food works for booking your next guesthouse too.


## Is there anything that will trip me up the first time?


Two small things. First, double-check the merchant name on the confirmation screen at busy stalls, because codes from neighboring carts sometimes sit close together. Second, the riel amounts look alarming to new arrivals because of all the zeros, so lean on the review screen, which shows you what the payment means in your own currency before you commit. Everything else is genuinely as simple as it looks when you watch a local do it.
